concept.name: Clearing member
concept.definition: A clearing member is a firm admitted to membership in a clearing organization (CCP) that clears trades directly through it. All trades of non-clearing members must be processed and settled through a clearing member, which is responsible to the CCP for the obligations — margin, settlement, and default contributions — of the trades it clears.
concept.intuition: A clearing member is the clearing house's guarantor: only these vetted, capitalized firms deal directly with the CCP, and everyone else's trades reach the CCP through them.
concept.mechanics: Clearing members meet the CCP's financial and operational admission standards, post margin and default-fund contributions, and guarantee the performance of their own and their clients' cleared trades. At futures exchanges, clearing members are often FCMs; customer positions of non-members are carried on a clearing member's books.
concept.failure_modes: A clearing member guarantees client trades, so a client's default can sink the member, and a member's default cascades risk into the CCP's waterfall. Concentration of client clearing in a few large members amplifies systemic exposure.
concept.misconceptions: Exchange trading membership and clearing membership are distinct — a firm may trade on an exchange without clearing there. End customers of a clearing member are not protected by the CCP directly; their recourse runs through the member and customer-segregation rules.
concept.example: A small proprietary trading firm is not a clearing member, so it clears its futures trades through an FCM that is a clearing member of the exchange's clearing house and posts margin to the CCP on the firm's behalf.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
